templates.title: Check-in could not be scored
templates.whatChanged: This session did not pass quality checks, so it was not added to your personal baseline.
templates.whyItMatters: A short or interrupted test cannot give a reliable response speed on the 3-minute PVT-B.
whatToDo: Settle into a quiet spot with the same device and posture.
Run the 3-minute check-in again when ready.

templates.title: Learning your personal normal
templates.whatChanged: This check-in is saved, and your personal baseline is still building.
templates.whyItMatters: The 3-minute PVT-B shows little practice effect, so a handful of rested sessions set a steady personal normal.
whatToDo: Keep taking your morning check-in on the same device.
Your personal normal band will appear after enough valid sessions.

templates.title: Slower than your normal for {days} days in a row
templates.whatChanged: Your reaction speed is {zAbs} SD below your own normal, with {lapses} lapses, for {days} consecutive check-ins.
templates.whyItMatters: ISS astronauts whose PVT speed falls at or below 1.5 SD from their baseline show meaningful cognitive slowing.
whatToDo: Put off precision or safety-critical tasks that can wait.
Tell a crewmate and ask them to double-check key steps.
Prioritise rest and check your blood pressure if you feel unwell.

templates.title: Slower than your normal after short sleep
templates.whatChanged: Your reaction speed is {zAbs} SD below your own normal. You slept {sleepHours} hours.
templates.whyItMatters: On the ISS, reaction speed on this test was slower after 6 hours of sleep or less.
whatToDo: Put off precision tasks that can wait.
Ask a crewmate to double-check critical steps today.
Plan a full sleep period tonight.
Repeat the check-in tomorrow morning.

templates.title: Slower than your personal normal
templates.whatChanged: Your reaction speed is {zAbs} SD below your own normal, with {lapses} lapses.
templates.whyItMatters: On the ISS Cognition battery, PVT speed at or below 1.5 SD from baseline marks low alertness.
whatToDo: Put off precision tasks that can wait.
Ask a crewmate to double-check critical procedures today.
Repeat the check-in tomorrow morning.

templates.title: Slightly below your personal normal
templates.whatChanged: Your reaction speed is {zAbs} SD below your own normal, with {lapses} lapses.
templates.whyItMatters: Tracking small dips on the 3-minute PVT-B gives an early heads-up before performance falls further.
whatToDo: Pace demanding work and build in short breaks.
Aim for a full sleep period tonight.
Repeat the check-in tomorrow morning.

templates.title: Within your personal normal
templates.whatChanged: Your reaction speed is within your recent normal range, with {lapses} lapses.
templates.whyItMatters: Staying near your own PVT-B baseline reflects steady vigilant attention.
whatToDo: Continue your normal schedule.
Repeat the check-in tomorrow morning.

templates.title: Very high blood pressure with warning symptoms
templates.whatChanged: Your reading averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg with warning symptoms.
templates.whyItMatters: Blood pressure above 180/120 mmHg paired with acute symptoms requires immediate action without waiting.
whatToDo: Stop activity and alert a crewmate now. Do not wait for Earth.
Do not wait to retest when symptoms are present.
Log the symptoms and readings for crew medical review.

templates.title: Low blood pressure with symptoms
templates.whatChanged: Your reading averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg with low-pressure symptoms.
templates.whyItMatters: Blood pressure below 90/60 mmHg with symptoms like dizziness or fainting can signal inadequate blood flow.
whatToDo: Lie down right away and alert a crewmate.
Open the dizzy or near-fainting emergency steps if you are alert.
Do not wait for Earth if symptoms worsen.

templates.title: Confirmed very high blood pressure
templates.whatChanged: Your retest averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg, still above 180/120 mmHg.
templates.whyItMatters: A repeated reading above 180/120 mmHg confirms severe hypertension requiring prompt medical attention.
whatToDo: Rest quietly and alert a crewmate now.
Do not wait for Earth if any new symptom appears.
Queue this reading for flight surgeon review.

templates.title: Very high reading: measure again
templates.whatChanged: Your reading averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg. Above 180/120 is in the severe range.
templates.whyItMatters: One very high reading can be a measurement error. The guidance is to wait and measure again, unless you have symptoms.
whatToDo: Rest quietly for about 5 minutes.
Take the measurement again.
If you get chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness or weakness, a change in vision or trouble speaking, alert a crewmate now.

templates.title: Sustained high blood pressure across {days} days
templates.whatChanged: Your average reading of {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg marks {days} separate days at or above 140/90 mmHg.
templates.whyItMatters: NASA spaceflight standards define hypertension as sustained blood pressure at or above 140/90 mmHg.
whatToDo: Avoid heavy exertion until reviewed.
Share your recent log with a crewmate and queue for flight surgeon review.
Take another guided check tomorrow.

templates.title: High blood pressure (stage 2)
templates.whatChanged: Your reading averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg, which is in the stage 2 range (140/90 mmHg or higher).
templates.whyItMatters: Readings at or above 140/90 mmHg are classified as stage 2 hypertension in AHA/ACC guidelines.
whatToDo: Take a follow-up guided check on another day to watch for a pattern.
Note any unusual stress, salt intake, or poor sleep.
Watch for warning symptoms.

templates.title: Low blood pressure reading
templates.whatChanged: Your reading averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg, below 90/60 mmHg without reported symptoms.
templates.whyItMatters: NHLBI defines low blood pressure as lower than 90/60 mmHg, which merits monitoring even without symptoms.
whatToDo: Move slowly when changing posture and hydrate steadily.
Open the near-fainting guide if you start feeling dizzy.
Repeat the check if you notice any symptoms.

templates.title: Different from your in-flight normal
templates.whatChanged: Your systolic pressure of {systolic} mmHg is {zAbs} SD away from your own in-flight baseline.
templates.whyItMatters: On the ISS, 24-hour blood pressure typically sits about 8/9 mmHg lower than pre-flight, so shifts from your own in-flight normal stand out earlier.
whatToDo: Check that the cuff fit and rest steps were followed.
Repeat a guided measurement over the next few days to see if the shift holds.

templates.title: Slightly above normal blood pressure
templates.whatChanged: Your reading averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg, in the elevated or stage 1 range.
templates.whyItMatters: AHA/ACC categories classify 120–129/<80 as elevated and 130–139 or 80–89 as stage 1.
whatToDo: Continue routine guided blood pressure checks.
Keep a quiet 5-minute rest before measuring.

templates.title: Blood pressure within normal range
templates.whatChanged: Your reading averaged {systolic}/{diastolic} mmHg, within the normal range and your personal baseline.
templates.whyItMatters: Readings below 120/80 mmHg align with normal AHA/ACC blood pressure categories.
whatToDo: Continue your regular check-in routine.
